criteria: The class `TaskQueue` is implemented in `pqueue.py`, and a new `TaskQueue()` is empty.

`TaskQueue.push(item, priority=0)` adds `item` and returns its ticket, an `int`; the first push on a queue returns 1 and each later push returns one more than the push before it, whatever was popped or cancelled in between.
`TaskQueue.pop()` removes and returns the item with the highest priority; priorities are `int`s, a larger number is a higher priority, and priorities may be negative.
In `TaskQueue`, among items of equal priority, the one that was pushed first comes out first.
`TaskQueue.peek()` returns the item that `pop()` would return and leaves it in the queue; `pop()` and `peek()` raise `IndexError` when the queue is empty.
`len(queue)` on a `TaskQueue` is the number of items waiting in the queue.

`TaskQueue.cancel(ticket)` removes the item with that ticket and returns `True`; when the ticket is not waiting (it was never issued, or its item was already popped or cancelled) it returns `False` and changes nothing.

`TaskQueue.reprioritize(ticket, priority)` gives a waiting item a new priority and returns `None`; the item keeps its place in push order, so among items of its new priority it comes out before those pushed after it and after those pushed before it (e.g. after `a = queue.push("a")`, `queue.push("b")`, `queue.push("c", 5)` and `queue.reprioritize(a, 5)` the pops give `"a"`, `"c"`, `"b"`); a ticket that is not waiting raises `KeyError`.

`TaskQueue` never compares items with each other and never hashes them, so the queue works with items such as dicts; the same item may be pushed more than once, and each push is a separate entry with its own ticket.
